chapters.title: One name, three different evaluations
chapters.lede: EASE (Eduversal Analytical & Skills Evaluation) is not one test. It is an umbrella for three separate systems, each with its own purpose, audience and use of scores.

blocks.lead: EASE tells your school **how students think, what they have learned, and where teachers want to grow** — three questions, three tools, kept apart.
points: **EASE Growth** — students' reasoning and literacy. Not based on the curriculum, never graded.
**EASE Assessment** (also called **Common Assessment**) — what students learned in class. It counts in the gradebook.
**EASE Academic** — teachers' subject and teaching knowledge, for professional development only.
Keep the three **separate** in purpose, communication, score use and follow-up.

chapters.lede: Two EASE Weeks in each semester. In the mid-semester weeks lessons continue; in the semester-end weeks lessons stop for the network test block. Your grade tab in the live EASE Schedule is always the final word.

items.sub: The three systems on one page

blocks.title: Common questions

items.q: Is “EASE Assessment” the same as “Common Assessment”?
items.a: Yes. Two names, one programme — both are correct.

items.q: If a student scores low on EASE Growth, does it affect their grade?
items.a: No. EASE Growth is never graded. It shows where a student may need support in reasoning or reading. This year the result is a baseline, not a growth score.

items.q: What happened to Mid-Term and Final Exams?
items.a: For Grades 7–12 they became EASE Assessment (Common Assessment): Teacher-Paced Tests through the year and Synchronized Tests at semester end, recorded in one Common Assessment category.

items.q: Can our school move a Synchronized Test?
items.a: No. Synchronized Tests are fixed across the network. The only exception is shown in the live EASE Schedule, where a Cambridge examination replaces the test for a grade and subject.

items.q: Can I see my teachers' EASE Academic scores?
items.a: No. Individual scores are confidential to each teacher. You receive school-level trends for professional development planning only.
Subject Specialists write them, the Academic Board reviews and approves them, and the Chief Academic Officer gives final sign-off before anything is published on Latihan.id.
